notes: Permission to appeal refused on fraud challenge to interlocutory costs order after Part 36 settlement of defamation claim.

enrichment.short_title: Pell v Express Newspapers: permission to appeal on alleged fraudulent redactions
key_facts: Benjamin Pell sued Express Newspapers and journalist Mark Watts over Sunday Express articles linking him to Bloody Sunday soldier names and the IRA; the action settled for £125,000 plus costs on the eve of trial.
Eady J refused late permission to re-amend for exemplary damages alleging a dishonest conspiracy with film-makers and declined to order disclosure of redacted telephone records and emails.
After settlement Pell obtained unredacted material showing Kevin Cahill's involvement and a nine-minute call to Cahill on 6 February 2002, which he said proved dishonest concealment in disclosure.
Pell sought permission to appeal nearly a year out of time solely to reverse the interlocutory costs orders of about £34,000 to defendants and £26,000 to himself, without disturbing the settlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against Eady J's refusal of re-amendment and further disclosure in a settled defamation action, relying on alleged new evidence of fraud.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the application was disproportionate, out of time, and the alleged fraud was hotly disputed and should be pursued by fresh action if at all.
enrichment.ratio: A party who has settled a defamation action cannot proportionately reopen interlocutory merits and alleged disclosure fraud by appeal merely to reverse costs orders; where fraud is seriously disputed the proper course is a fresh action under Jonesco v Beard, not an appeal process relitigating a settled dispute.
legal_issues: Whether interlocutory costs orders survive a Part 36 settlement and may be challenged on appeal
Whether redacted journalistic source material amounted to deliberate fraud on the court
Whether new evidence satisfied Ladd v Marshall and justified extension of time
Whether section 10 Contempt of Court Act 1981 could be invoked against alleged dishonest redactions
linked_authorities: Couwenbergh v Valkova [2004] EWCA Civ 676
Jonesco v Beard [1930] AC 298
Goodwin v United Kingdom (1996) 22 EHRR 123
Ashworth Hospital Authority v MGN Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 2033

confidence.notes: Rix LJ's detailed judgment sets out facts, authorities and refusal reasons clearly.

notes: Commercial Court preliminary issues on RWE's nuclear business purchase warranty and indemnity claims.

enrichment.short_title: RWE Nukem v AEAT: preliminary issues on warranty notification and indemnities
key_facts: RWE bought AEAT's nuclear engineering business for £23.7 million under a June 2001 agreement with extensive warranties qualified by a disclosure letter.
Schedule 9 required written particulars of warranty claims within 24 months of completion; RWE's September 2003 letter listed 19 complaints the day before expiry.
RWE pursued eight remaining warranty claims and indemnities under Schedule 19 relating to major contracts including pensions, KFK Sodium and PFR LMD.
AEAT contended several claims were demurrable, inadequately notified, or misconceived as to damages, timing and offset provisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of four preliminary issues in the Commercial Court on breach of warranty and indemnity claims arising from a business sale agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Damages for missed negotiation opportunities struck out; pensions and KFK Sodium claims held inadequately notified; PFR LMD notification claim succeeded but was later abandoned; indemnity timing and offset issues resolved largely in AEAT's favour.
enrichment.ratio: Warranty damages put the buyer in the position the promise was fulfilled, not the position if better terms had been negotiated; a notification clause requiring particulars of claims must identify the warranty breached, supporting facts and loss with sufficient clarity; Schedule 19 deemed recovery sums operate as mandatory offsets reducing indemnity payments.
legal_issues: Whether warranty damages could reflect lost opportunity to negotiate better deal terms
Whether the September 2003 letter complied with paragraph 2.4 of Schedule 9
When AEAT's Schedule 19 indemnity liability crystallised for the PFR LMD contract
Whether paragraph 7.3.2–7.3.5 sums were offsets or recovery thresholds
linked_authorities: Senate Electrical v STC [1999] 2 Lloyd's Rep 423
Laminates Acquisition Co v BTR Australia Ltd [2003] EWHC 2540
Bottin (International) Investments Ltd v Venson Group Plc [2004] EWCA Civ 1368
Lion Nathan v CC Bottlers [1996] 1 WLR 1438

confidence.notes: Gloster J's detailed rulings on each preliminary issue are explicit though some claims were abandoned post-judgment.

notes: Article 3 challenge to refusal of compassionate release for terminally ill life prisoner; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: R (Spinks): compassionate release and Article 3 for terminally ill lifer
key_facts: Clive Spinks was serving life for murder with parole eligibility from 2008 but was diagnosed with terminal colon cancer in October 2003.
He complained that prison disrupted chemotherapy, involved handcuffing at hospital, colostomy care difficulties and prevented hospice day attendance.
The Secretary of State refused compassionate release under section 30, applying published criteria including imminent death, incapacity and negligible re-offending risk.
Medical evidence indicated Spinks remained mobile and self-caring and that neither hospital nor full hospice admission was yet indicated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Elias J's refusal of judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision not to release a life prisoner on compassionate grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no breach of Article 3 was established and section 30(2) did not require Parole Board consultation before a decision not to release.
enrichment.ratio: Section 30(2) obliges consultation with the Parole Board only before releasing a life prisoner, not before deciding against release; where Article 3 is arguable the court must intensely review whether detention is incompatible, but adverse prison conditions for a terminally ill prisoner did not here reach Article 3 severity, distinguishing Mouisel v France.
legal_issues: Construction of section 30 Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 and the Parole Board's role
Whether continuing detention of a terminally ill prisoner breached Article 3 ECHR
Whether an arguable Article 3 breach required referral to the Parole Board for investigation
Application of Mouisel v France to handcuffing and medical care in prison
linked_authorities: Mouisel v France (2004) 38 EHRR 34
Wright v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 520
R (Amin) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 AC 653
R (ProLife Alliance) v BBC [2004] 1 AC 185

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on section 30, Article 3 and Mouisel comparison is clearly recorded.

notes: TCC preliminary issues on open-book construction contract and Target Order Value cost control regime.

enrichment.short_title: S & W v Cauldron Foods: Target Order Values and cost control on food plant contract
key_facts: S & W contracted to supply and install food processing plant at Cauldron's Bristol premises under an open-book arrangement evidenced by April–June 2002 correspondence.
The parties agreed Target Order Values totalling about £4.6 million with a procedure for authorising scope changes and overspends at weekly review meetings.
After early Cost Reports near the target figure, later invoices pushed the claimed sum toward £584,000 above agreed payments; Cauldron counterclaimed for defects.
The parties later dispensed with written Authorisation for Capital Expenditure certificates but retained oral authorisation at project meetings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues in the Technology and Construction Court on formation, express terms, target costs and authorisation of additional expenditure.
enrichment.outcome: Contract held to be open-book cost-plus subject to a £4,599,108.81 base Target Order Value; increases required prior oral agreement at weekly meetings; ACE forms were not a condition precedent to payment; quantum meruit claims were largely unavailable.
enrichment.ratio: Target Order Values were contractual ceiling figures forming part of a mandatory cost-control regime, not mere monitoring aspirations; additional work or overspends required discussion and agreement before financial commitment, initially via ACE certificates and after variation via minuted weekly meeting agreement.
legal_issues: Whether Target Order Values bound the employer's liability or were aspirational
Whether signed ACE forms were a condition precedent to payment
How additional work and overspends were to be authorised after ACE certificates fell into disuse
Availability of quantum meruit where contract governed the works
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Gloucestershire County Council v Richardson [1969] AC 480
Mowlem v Stena Line [2004] EWHC 2206

confidence.notes: Judge Coulson QC's findings on contract terms and preliminary issues are comprehensive and explicit.

notes: Appeal allowed on breach of licence sentence after Sharkey double-counting correction.

enrichment.short_title: R v Bennett: Sharkey adjustment for breach of licence sentence
key_facts: Bennett pleaded guilty to supplying heroin while on licence from a four-year sentence for earlier Class A drug offences.
He was sentenced to 502 days for breach of licence under section 116 and three years consecutive for the new offence.
The sentencing judge lacked accurate information on days served on administrative recall under section 39 before the licence expiry date.
An agreed chronology showed 205 days on administrative recall with licence expiry on 29 August 2004 after periods unlawfully at large.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the single judge against the section 116 breach of licence sentence only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; 502 days substituted with 92 days for breach of licence, subject to recalculation if licence expiry was earlier than assumed.
enrichment.ratio: Days spent in custody following administrative recall under section 39 before the licence expiry date must be doubled when calculating a section 116 return-to-custody sentence because section 116 custody is treated as an independent sentence normally served at half; prosecutors should obtain precise prison service recall data before sentencing.
legal_issues: How to calculate section 116 breach of licence sentence where section 39 recall periods apply
Effect of time unlawfully at large on licence expiry date
Whether approximate recall information suffices at sentencing
linked_authorities: Sharkey [2000] 1 Cr App R(S) 409
Stocker [2003] Crim LR 293
Teasdale [2003] Crim LR 657
Rady [2004] EWCA Crim 3297

confidence.notes: Outcome and Sharkey arithmetic are clear though final licence expiry remained subject to a caveat.

notes: First instance rejection of challenge to validity of Parliament Act 1949 and Hunting Act 2004.

enrichment.short_title: Jackson v Attorney General: validity of Parliament Act 1949 and Hunting Act
key_facts: The Hunting Bill was passed by the Commons in two sessions but rejected in amended form by the Lords; the Speaker certified compliance with the Parliament Acts and Royal Assent followed in November 2004.
Countryside Alliance members challenged the Hunting Act on the ground that the 1949 Act, which reduced the 1911 Act's session and time requirements, was not validly enacted.
The claimants argued the 1911 Act could not amend itself, that Acts under it were delegated legislation, and that a subordinate legislature could not expand its own powers.
Historical context included enactment of the Welsh Church Act 1914 and Government of Ireland Act 1914 under the unamended 1911 procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for declarations that the Parliament Act 1949 and Hunting Act 2004 are not valid Acts of Parliament.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the 1949 Act was validly passed under section 2 of the 1911 Act and the Hunting Act was lawfully promulgated; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(1) of the Parliament Act 1911 permits any Public Bill, subject to express exclusions, to become an Act of Parliament without Lords consent; such Acts are primary legislation creating an alternative legislative route, not delegated legislation, and may include a Bill amending the 1911 Act itself.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 of the 1911 Act authorises amendment of the 1911 Act without Lords consent
Whether legislation under the Parliament Acts is delegated or primary legislation
Whether colonial constitutional limits on subordinate legislatures apply
Justiciability of the Speaker's certificate under section 3
linked_authorities: Pickin v British Railways Board [1974] AC 765
The Queen v Burah (1878) 3 App Cas 889
Bribery Commissioner v Ranasinghe [1965] AC 172
Attorney General v Prince of Hanover [1957] AC 436

confidence.notes: Landmark first-instance judgment with full reasoning on all three grounds; later appealed to the House of Lords.

notes: Post-appeal costs ruling on representation orders and recovery of defence costs orders.

enrichment.short_title: R v K and others: recovery of defence costs after failed appeal
key_facts: The Court had dismissed the appellants' appeal on 2 November 2004 and listed a further hearing on costs.
Appellants K and G had failed to lodge means forms before the appeal; G cited absence in the Far East for seven weeks.
Representation orders cover only grounds for which leave was granted, not failed renewed applications for leave.
K had £112,000 equity in his home; M had £205,000 equity; G disclosed limited means and a £350,000 High Court judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary judgment on costs following dismissal of a Court of Appeal criminal appeal, including representation order scope and recovery of defence costs.
enrichment.outcome: Registrar to assess split fee notes; K ordered to contribute from equity above £100,000; M to contribute from house equity; G referred to Legal Services Commission for means investigation; late form lodging practice criticised.
enrichment.ratio: A Court of Appeal representation order extends only to grounds on which leave was granted and fee notes must split appeal and renewed application work; failed appellants with means should contribute via recovery of defence costs orders and advocates must lodge accurate means forms promptly.
legal_issues: Scope of Court of Appeal representation orders where renewed leave applications fail
Whether grant of leave precludes a recovery of defence costs order
Contribution from home equity where legally aided appellants fail
Procedure when means forms are not lodged before appeal

confidence.notes: Practice directions on representation orders and costs are clear though underlying appeal merits are not rehearsed.

notes: Contempt committal quashed after wife's false post-hearing assault allegation undermined credibility.

enrichment.short_title: Champken: contempt appeal quashed after complainant's false police report
key_facts: John Champken faced committal for breaching non-molestation injunctions obtained after alleged domestic violence toward Vanessa Champken and their children.
Judge Mott on 29 April 2004 found breaches and imposed a suspended four-month committal; Judge Coles on 20 May 2004 found further breaches and imposed six months suspended.
On 21 May 2004, the day after Judge Coles' hearing, Mrs Champken falsely told police she was assaulted by a man saying 'John said you don't think he's going to leave you alone'.
She admitted the allegation was entirely false the same night and later pleaded guilty to attempting to pervert the course of justice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against committal orders for contempt of court in county court family injunction proceedings, with fresh evidence admitted on appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; committal orders of Judge Coles and Judge Mott quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: A committal decision may be overturned on appeal where fresh evidence shows the complainant's credibility was fundamentally tainted, especially when a false allegation strikingly similar to earlier complaints is fabricated immediately after the judge believed her evidence.
legal_issues: Test for interfering with factual findings in contempt proceedings
Admissibility and effect of fresh evidence of a false post-hearing complaint
Whether misspelling of 'lying' in a threatening letter undermined specific breach findings
linked_authorities: Abouchitaa v El-Yamlahi [2001] EWCA Civ 1407

confidence.notes: Laws LJ's reasoning on unsafe committal driven by fresh false allegation is explicit.

notes: Attorney General's reference; Scott's cocaine sentence increased, Holmes' lenient sentence not disturbed.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: unduly lenient cocaine supply sentences for undercover operation runners
key_facts: Cleveland police ran an undercover operation at a Stockton pub targeting cocaine supply; Holmes supplied on 14 occasions over 12 months for £7,600 and Scott supplied on eight occasions over two months for £30,000.
Both pleaded guilty on the day of trial to being concerned in supplying cocaine; co-conspirator Wascoe received eight years for conspiracy.
Scott had previous convictions including firearms and cocaine possession; Holmes was of previous good character and a recreational user acting as intermediary.
Judge Spittal sentenced Scott to three-and-a-half years and Holmes to three years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences for concerned-in-supply offences.
enrichment.outcome: Scott's sentence increased from three-and-a-half to five years; Holmes' three-year sentence, though lenient, was not interfered with because of double jeopardy and his four months already at liberty.
enrichment.ratio: Repeated large-scale supply of cocaine to undercover officers over months warrants substantially higher sentences for runners closely involved in distribution; double jeopardy and time already served may justify leaving a lenient but not unduly lenient sentence undisturbed.
legal_issues: Whether Scott's and Holmes' sentences were unduly lenient for concerned-in-supply of cocaine
Relevance of role as runner, quantity supplied and period of dealing
Whether Holmes fell within Afonso principles for addict retail suppliers
Effect of double jeopardy and early release on reference outcome
linked_authorities: R v Afonso [2004] EWCA Crim 2342
R v Dhajit [1999] 2 Cr App R(S) 142
R v Twisse [2001] 2 Cr App R(S) 37
R v Williams [2000] 2 Cr App R(S) 308

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating features and differentiated outcomes for Scott and Holmes are clearly stated.

notes: School exclusion appeal panel decision upheld; reinstatement guidance and reasons considered.

enrichment.short_title: R (Q) v Wolverhampton panel: school exclusion appeal and reinstatement
key_facts: Pupil A was permanently excluded after kicking a youth on the ground during a violent incident at school involving multiple assailants and injuring a caretaker who intervened.
An independent appeal panel upheld the appeal against permanent exclusion but declined reinstatement, citing breakdown in relations between pupil, teachers, family and other pupils.
Witness statements had been anonymised for fear of reprisal; the headteacher requested a security escort when leaving the hearing.
Guidance required panels considering non-reinstatement to establish whether an irretrievable breakdown existed and to give reasons in the decision letter.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an independent school exclusion appeal panel's decision to overturn permanent exclusion but not direct reinstatement.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no procedural unfairness in how reinstatement was considered and supplementary panel material adequately explained the irretrievable breakdown conclusion despite an inadequate decision letter.
enrichment.ratio: A panel may elicit evidence on reinstatement during the hearing and in final submissions without a separate discrete hearing provided parties have a fair opportunity to respond; where reinstatement is refused for irretrievable breakdown, inadequate decision letter reasons may be cured by undisputed hearing material showing ample basis for the conclusion.
legal_issues: Whether the panel complied with guidance on irretrievable breakdown before refusing reinstatement
Whether fairness required a discrete hearing on reinstatement after overturning exclusion
Whether the headteacher's post-hearing security request was improperly taken into account
Sufficiency of reasons in the decision letter for non-reinstatement

confidence.notes: Newman J's detailed analysis of fairness and reasons is thorough though some procedural facts were contested.
